title: Esther 6:1–11
context: Esther 6:1–11 describes a sleepless night that turns the story. The king cannot sleep and has the royal chronicles read to him. They record how Mordecai exposed the plot of Bigthana and Teresh against the king (2:21–23), and the king learns that nothing was done to honor him. At that moment Haman arrives to ask permission to hang Mordecai on the gallows he has built (5:14). Asked what should be done for the man the king delights to honor, Haman assumes he means himself and describes a royal procession. The king then orders Haman to do all of it for Mordecai the Jew, and Haman must lead Mordecai through the city square proclaiming his honor. The book of Esther never names God, and the narrator gives no explanation for the timing. Readers in both traditions commonly see God’s hidden providence in this sequence of events, and that reading is shared ground. The text, however, simply tells the story without comment, and these notes avoid reading more into the details than the narrative gives.

verses.text: On that night, the king couldn’t sleep. He commanded the book of records of the chronicles to be brought, and they were read to the king.
verses.arminianNotes: On that night the king cannot sleep, and he orders the chronicles to be read to him. Arminian readers often see God’s hidden hand in the timing, while noting that the book does not name God and the king’s choices remain his own.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s providence ordering even a king’s sleepless night. Both traditions treat the hidden-providence reading as shared ground, and both note that the narrator records the event without explaining it, so they avoid overreading it.

verses.text: It was found written that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king’s eunuchs, who were doorkeepers, who had tried to lay hands on the King Ahasuerus.
verses.arminianNotes: The record shows that Mordecai had reported Bigthana and Teresh, two doorkeepers who tried to harm King Ahasuerus. Arminians see faithful service, long forgotten, coming back to light at the right moment (compare 2:21–23).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s timing in bringing this record forward. Both traditions read the verse as part of the turning point of the story, and they recognize that the narrator lets the sequence of events speak for itself.

verses.text: The king said, “What honor and dignity has been given to Mordecai for this?” Then the king’s servants who attended him said, “Nothing has been done for him.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king asks what honor Mordecai received, and his servants say nothing was done. Arminian readers see an injustice about to be corrected, and they note how Mordecai’s earlier loyalty went unrewarded.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the delay as preparing a more striking reversal. Both traditions treat the verse as shared ground, and they avoid claiming to know why the reward was delayed, since the text does not say.

verses.text: The king said, “Who is in the court?” Now Haman had come into the outer court of the king’s house, to speak to the king about hanging Mordecai on the gallows that he had prepared for him.
verses.arminianNotes: The king asks who is in the court, and Haman has just arrived to ask about hanging Mordecai on the gallows he had built. Arminians see the dramatic irony of Haman arriving to destroy the very man the king now wants to honor.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the timing as part of the providential pattern many readers find in Esther. Both traditions note the narrator’s skill in bringing the two plans together, without adding comment the text does not make.

verses.text: The king’s servants said to him, “Behold, Haman stands in the court.” The king said, “Let him come in.”
verses.arminianNotes: The servants tell the king that Haman is standing in the court, and the king tells them to bring him in. Arminian readers see the scene being set for Haman’s own words to lead to his humiliation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as a simple narrative link. Both traditions see it as moving the story toward the reversal in which Haman must honor Mordecai.

verses.text: So Haman came in. The king said to him, “What shall be done to the man whom the king delights to honor?” Now Haman said in his heart, “Who would the king delight to honor more than myself?”
verses.arminianNotes: The king asks what should be done for the man he delights to honor, and Haman thinks it must be himself. Arminians see pride blinding Haman, so that he assumes the honor is his and plans his own humiliation.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the verse as a vivid picture of self-centered pride. Both traditions compare the scene with Proverbs 16:18 and read it as shared ground about pride going before a fall.

verses.text: Haman said to the king, “For the man whom the king delights to honor,
verses.arminianNotes: Haman begins his answer to the king about the man the king delights to honor. Arminian readers see him speaking with eagerness, expecting to receive what he describes, which heightens the irony of the scene.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as the start of Haman’s self-serving proposal. Both traditions see the narrative inviting readers to notice how his ambition will turn against him.

verses.text: let royal clothing be brought which the king uses to wear, and the horse that the king rides on, and on the head of which a royal crown is set.
verses.arminianNotes: Haman proposes royal clothing the king has worn and the king’s own horse with a royal crown on its head. Arminians see Haman seeking honor that comes close to sharing royal status, which reveals his ambition.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the request as showing how deeply Haman craved glory. Both traditions note that the phrase about the crown may refer to the horse’s head, and they read the verse as part of Haman’s proposal without building on the detail.

verses.text: Let the clothing and the horse be delivered to the hand of one of the king’s most noble princes, that they may array the man whom the king delights to honor with them, and have him ride on horseback through the city square, and proclaim before him, ‘Thus it shall be done to the man whom the king delights to honor!’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Haman proposes that a noble prince dress the honored man and lead him through the city square, proclaiming his honor. Arminian readers see Haman designing a public display of glory for himself, which he will instead give to his enemy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the coming reversal as fitting judgment on pride. Both traditions read the verse as shared ground about the danger of seeking one’s own glory.

verses.text: Then the king said to Haman, “Hurry and take the clothing and the horse, as you have said, and do this for Mordecai the Jew, who sits at the king’s gate. Let nothing fail of all that you have spoken.”
verses.arminianNotes: The king tells Haman to hurry and do all of it for Mordecai the Jew who sits at the king’s gate. Arminians see a stunning reversal, as Haman must honor the man he planned to kill.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the reversal as part of the providential pattern of the book. Both traditions note that the king names Mordecai as a Jew, which echoes the central conflict of the story, and they read the verse as shared ground.

verses.text: Then Haman took the clothing and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai, and had him ride through the city square, and proclaimed before him, “Thus it shall be done to the man whom the king delights to honor!”
verses.arminianNotes: Haman dresses Mordecai, leads him through the city square, and proclaims his honor. Arminian readers see the proud man humbled and the faithful man honored, a theme found throughout Scripture.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s justice at work, though the book itself does not name him. Both traditions read the scene as a reversal that anticipates Haman’s downfall, and they avoid embellishing it beyond the text.
